activities.anchor: The Grand Canyon is a kilometre of rock removed
activities.caption: call the size of the planet's biggest sediment pile
activities.name: weatherFanEst

config.prompt: The Himalaya's erosion feeds the Bengal Fan on the Indian Ocean floor — how thick is that sediment cone?
config.why: About 16 km thick — the largest body of sediment on the planet, built entirely from the Himalaya's demolition.
config.context: the Grand Canyon, by comparison, is a kilometre of rock removed

activities.caption: file each process under the weathering it belongs to
activities.name: weatherProcSort

config.prompt: File each process under the weathering it belongs to:
config.why: Mechanical weathering multiplies surfaces; chemical weathering consumes them — and each accelerates the other.

activities.anchor: attacks the minerals themselves, and rainwater is
activities.caption: pair each reaction with its landscape signature
activities.name: weatherChemMatch

config.prompt: Pair each chemical reaction with its landscape signature:

pairs.right: karst — caves, sinkholes and disappearing streams
clay, the most abundant weathering product on Earth
the reds and browns of weathered rock and soil

pairs.left: rain absorbing CO₂ as it falls

config.why: Rainwater is the reagent; each reaction leaves a readable signature on the landscape.

activities.caption: drop the marker — the frost wedge's leverage
activities.name: weatherFrostPlace

config.prompt: Water expands by about what percentage when it freezes — the pry bar of frost wedging?
config.why: About 9% — repeated nightly through a mountain winter, prying with forces up to roughly 200 MPa, enough to split granite.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — the three ways a stream hauls
activities.name: weatherLoadCloze

config.text: A stream carries its cargo three ways: %%0%% rolling along the bottom, %%1%% drifting with the current, and %%2%% invisible in the water itself.
config.hint: One rolls, one rides, one vanishes into the water chemistry.

activities.caption: find the backwards claim — what ice refuses to do
activities.name: weatherIceSpot

config.prompt: One of these claims about glacier transport is backwards — click it:
lines: Glacier ice drags frozen debris across bedrock under hundreds of metres of its own weight.
It plucks blocks loose and polishes what remains with rock-flour.
Its valleys are U-shaped where streams cut V-shaped ones.
Moraine and till are well sorted, finest grains first.
config.correction: Moraine and till are a chaotic mix from clay to house-sized boulders — ice does not sort.
config.why: The size law belongs to water; ice is the one sediment where sorting conspicuously fails.

config.prompt: Rebuild the coast's slow straightening — what happens first:
items: Waves refract and focus their energy on the protruding headland
A sea cave is eroded from both sides of the headland
The cave cuts through — an arch stands
The arch collapses, leaving a resistant stack
config.why: Headlands erode faster, and an irregular coast slowly straightens itself into cliffs, wave-cut platforms and stacks.

activities.caption: run the flood — decide what settles where
activities.name: weatherFloodBranch

config.root: A river bursts its banks onto a floodplain. What settles where?

start.text: The flow leaves the channel and suddenly slows.

choices.label: Coarse gravel drops right at the channel; clay travels farthest
choices.feedback: The size law at work: fast flows carry big particles, slow flows only fine ones.

choices.label: Fine clay drops first — it is the lightest
choices.feedback: Backwards: clay stays suspended longest and settles farthest out.

choices.label: Nothing settles — the flood carries everything to the sea
choices.feedback: Some does — but the floodplain keeps its silt, which is why floodplains are farmland.

backwards.text: Watch a jar of muddy water settle: big grains first, clay last.

choices.label: Re-answer: the coarse load drops where the flow brakes
choices.feedback: Right — biggest first, at the point the current slows.

law.text: The fan, the floodplain and the delta all run on this one law.

partial.text: The floodplain keeps its silt either way — deposition by size, right where the water slowed.

config.why: Wherever a current brakes, it deposits by size — gravel → sand → silt → clay, with the dissolved load reaching the sea last.

activities.caption: pair each rock with its origin
activities.name: weatherRockMatch

config.prompt: Pair each sedimentary rock with its origin:

pairs.right: rounded gravel — a fast, short journey
mud compacted into fissile sheets — the calm deep-water record, the most abundant
calcite from warm shallow seas, much of it shell debris

config.why: Every sedimentary rock is a compressed photograph of a place and moment, stacked in order.

activities.anchor: Read a cliff as a worked example
activities.caption: bet before you read on — the cliff's one-sentence history
activities.name: weatherCliffPredict

config.q: A cliff runs, bottom to top: conglomerate, cross-bedded sandstone, mud-cracked shale, fossiliferous limestone. What single sentence of history does it tell?
choices: The land sank (or the sea rose), in that order
The sea dried up and the rocks were later flipped upside down
A glacier advanced and retreated four times
config.why: Five rock names, one sentence of history — the land sank or the sea rose, in that order, with superposition (younger layers on top) supplying the timeline the whole way up.
